1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zukertort Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.background: 2.Nf3 is the second most common move after 1.d4 d5, behind the Queen's Gambit 2.c4, and the position is also frequently reached via 1.Nf3.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and controls e4, while committing the c- and e-pawns to nothing yet. That flexibility is the strength and the cost: White still decides what kind of game it becomes, from a Queen's Gambit to quiet set-ups with an early bishop move.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and keeps the c8-bishop's route to f5 or g4 open, since ...e6 has not been played. It is solid and differs little from 2...Nf6 in most lines. The cost is that the b8-knight loses its natural c6-square.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop's diagonal, a solid set-up that differs little from 2...Nf6 in most lines. The cost is the c8-bishop, now shut in behind the e6-pawn, which usually has to wait for a fianchetto or a later central pawn break to find a diagonal.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: This is the knight move of the Chigorin Defence, 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6, named after the 19th-century Russian master Mikhail Chigorin and considered playable but rare. After 3.c4 this position transposes into that defence's 3.Nf3 line.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once and pressures d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so d5 can no longer be supported by ...c6. With only the queen guarding d5, White can hit it immediately with c4.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes it in, a mirror image of White's own bishop-first set-up. The cost is that the b7-pawn loses its only defender, and 3.Nh4 attacks the bishop at once, aiming to trade the knight for it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Anti-Torre
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop actively and prepares ...Bxf3, which would double White's f-pawns. But 3.Ne5 attacks the bishop and gains a tempo, and with the bishop gone from c8 the b7-pawn has no defender.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Krause Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5.background: Named after Orla Hermann Krause (1867–1935), a Danish chess master and analyst who found many new ideas in the Slav Defence in the 1920s. He played first board for Denmark at the 1927 London Olympiad, where the team won silver.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and brings tension into the centre instead of defending d5 passively. The cost is time and structure: if White takes on c5, Black must spend moves regaining the pawn, and d5 has little support meanwhile. It aims for an active game rather than a solid one.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop before the centre is settled. It is sound, but without …Nf6 or …c6 the d5-pawn has only the queen to guard it, so 3.c4 puts pressure on it at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nd7.strategy: Prepares ...e5 or ...c5 with the knight's support, which is sound. But it shuts in the c8-bishop and leaves d5 guarded by the queen alone, so White builds at ease.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but is far from the centre. It costs a tempo for little, and White can simply carry on building.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bd7.strategy: Puts the bishop on a passive square, where it blocks the queen and takes d7 from the b8-knight. White can continue with a free hand.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Be6.strategy: Shuts in the e-pawn, so …e6 is no longer possible. The bishop guards d5, but it invites 3.Ng5, which attacks it and threatens Nxe6 fxe6 to double Black's pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early and blocks the c8-bishop. 3.Ne5 attacks it at once and gains a tempo, with the d4-pawn guarding the knight.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to an exposed square. 3.Nc3 threatens Nb5, which would attack both the queen and c7.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Aims for f5 but invites 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which wrecks Black's kingside pawns into doubled, isolated h-pawns. The bishop pair is little compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: A flank move that prepares ...b5, which is sound but slow: it develops nothing and does nothing for the centre. White cannot punish it at once, but gains a free move.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Controls b4 without costing anything concrete, but develops nothing and leaves b5 without pawn cover. White gains a free move for the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which is sound, but that bishop would only look at Black's own d5-pawn until the centre opens, and c6 is weakened. White gains a free move to develop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Stops c4 for now but leaves the pawn loose: 3.e3 already threatens Bxb5+. It develops nothing and leaves c6 without pawn cover.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. White develops freely while Black's development lags behind.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Plays for a Dutch-style set-up, but the pawn weakens e6 and the king's diagonal and leaves e5 as an outpost for White's knight. Black must still develop all the pieces behind it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's bishop and knight, which is sound, but develops nothing. White uses the tempo to build in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Gains space on the flank at the cost of a tempo and the g5-square: the h-pawn can no longer drive a White piece from g5, and the advanced pawn can become a target.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.gxh3 wins a whole piece for nothing, since the bishop on h3 is attacked by the g2-pawn and defended by nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing and walks into 3.Ne5+, which forces the king to move again. Black loses more time, and the king stays stuck in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn for no clear return: after 3.dxe5 the pawn is gone, and ...d4 would lose a second one to Nxd4. Black has little to show against a White position without weaknesses.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 or 3.Nxg5 wins it, and the loosened kingside offers no compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, which is now attacked by the pawn and defended only by the queen. Black's early bishop move has not added a defender to d5, so Black must decide at once how to hold the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and mirrors Black's set-up. Sound, but it does nothing against the bishop on f5 or the centre, so Black develops freely and the game stays quiet and level.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.Nh4.strategy: Attacks the bishop with a knight on the rim. If the bishop retreats to g6, the knight can take it and leave Black with doubled g-pawns, but Black can also keep the bishop, and the knight on h4 has done little for White's development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6.strategy: Defends d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop. The c8-bishop is already outside the chain, so the usual worry about it being shut in by this move does not arise, and Black gets a solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 c6.strategy: Holds d5 with the c-pawn, a solid but slightly passive set-up. It leaves b7 without a defender once the queen comes to b3, which attacks it, so Black has to meet that threat at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, but the pawn is regained with the queen check on a4 or by simple development. Black has traded the d-pawn for the c-pawn and given up the centre, so White gets a free hand in the middle.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queenside knight and adds a second attacker to d5, so the pressure on Black's centre is now real. White has a sound set-up against the d-pawn, while Black's bishop is already outside the chain, so the fight is over whether d5 can be held.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6 4.Qb3.strategy: Attacks the b7 pawn, which has no defender now that the c8-bishop has left, and keeps the c4 pawn supported. Black has to spend a move on it, but the queen has come out early.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6 4.cxd5.strategy: Gives up the pressure on d5 that made c4 purposeful, in return for a half-open c-file. Black recaptures with the e-pawn and the bishop is already developed, so White has no immediate edge.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3.strategy: Guards d4 and opens the f1-bishop, a solid way to meet the c-pawn. The c1-bishop is closed in for now, so White chooses a quiet, flexible game over fighting for the initiative at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto and lets Black take on d4, which White intends to win back through development and pressure on the long diagonal. It declines to defend the centre pawn and allows Black to try to hold the extra one.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 at once, which Black's ...c5 has left without a pawn on c6 to support it. White fights for the centre as in a Queen's Gambit, usually reaching an open game in which the exchanges on d5 and c5 can leave Black with an isolated d-pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight supports d5 and controls e4, so White cannot easily establish a pawn there. Black keeps the tension on d4 with the c-pawn and develops without committing the other pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d4 and develops with it, so White has to keep the centre pawn guarded. The knight does nothing for d5, which only the queen guards, so Black must be ready for White's c-pawn to strike there.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, keeping a compact pawn chain. The c8-bishop is shut in for the moment, but the centre is sturdy and White has to challenge it with the c-pawn to get anything.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2.strategy: Develops the queenside knight to a square where it guards e4 and f3 and leaves the c-pawn free to move. The c1-bishop is now boxed in by the knight and the e3-pawn, so a pawn move will be needed to free it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.c3.strategy: Supports d4 a second time, so ...cxd4 can be answered by a recapture that keeps a pawn in the centre, and prepares the bishop on d3 and the knight on d2 behind it. White commits to a slow, solid build-up aimed at a well-timed e4 break later, and the game stays closed unless Black acts.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Bd3.strategy: Aims the bishop at h7 and the e4 square, so the central e4 break is prepared with the bishop already in place. The bishop blocks the d-file, so d4 is held only by the e3 pawn and the knight, and ...c4 hits the bishop at once and gains Black space.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, completing a compact centre of pawns on c5, d5 and e6. Black has a sound, flexible position in which White's quiet set-up gives no obvious target.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 Nc6.strategy: Piles up on d4 and develops in the same move, making White keep guarding the centre pawn while the c1-bishop is still shut in behind the knight and the e3 pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 cxd4.strategy: Clears the centre at once. After the usual exd4 White keeps the c-pawn and Black the e-pawn, so the game is quiet and balanced, and Black has given up the tension on d4 for it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 e6 5.b3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zukertort Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 e6 5.b3.strategy: Frees the c1-bishop, which the knight on d2 and the pawn on b2 had boxed in, so it can settle on b2 on the long diagonal and press on the centre. A modest but flexible set-up that keeps the pawn centre intact.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 e6 5.Bd.strategy: Aims the bishop at h7 and supports the e4 break, the plan of this set-up: with the knight on d2 already guarding e4, a well-timed e4 gives White the centre and open lines. The bishop blocks the d-file, and ...c4 can drive it back and gain Black space.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nbd2 e6 5.c3.strategy: Props up d4 and keeps the pawn centre firm if Black takes on d4. A patient move: the c1-bishop is still boxed in, so White develops slowly and relies on the solid structure.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 cxd4.strategy: Takes the centre pawn, which removes White's hold on the middle and wins a pawn for the moment. The pawn on d4 is only loosely held, so Black has to decide whether to keep it or return it for development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and adds a second attacker to d4, which g3 has left without extra support, so Black asks at once how White means to hold the centre. The pawn structure stays healthy and Black can still take on d4 when it suits.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, guarding d5 and e4, before deciding what to do with the pawn on d4. Black declines to grab it at once and keeps a flexible, solid centre that White has to challenge.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 cxd4 4.Bg2.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chandler Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 cxd4 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal and delays winning the pawn back: the pawn on d4 is attacked by the knight and queen and defended by nothing, so White can take it at once, but Black has time to support it with ...e5 or ...Nc6. As a gambit it asks little of Black.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with a piece, so material is level and the knight stands in the centre. Black can gain space by chasing it, but that costs time, and White's plan of g3 and a fianchettoed bishop is untouched.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5 3.g3 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once, which keeps material level, but ...Nc6 hits the queen and it has to move again (5.Qxd5 loses it to ...Qxd5). Black develops with a tempo, so White pays in time for a pawn it could regain without that cost.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the c1-bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, and makes an early ...Nf6 awkward because Bxf6 would double Black's pawns. The cost is that the bishop leaves the queenside, where b2 loses its guard.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.c4.strategy: The principal answer: the pawn challenges d5 and White fights for the centre from the start, while ...c6 gives Black a solid pawn chain. Black's usual aim is to bring the c8-bishop outside the chain, and the game becomes a rich fight in which development decides.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.e3.strategy: Solid and flexible: it opens the f1-bishop and supports d4, and keeps the c-pawn move for later. White gives up quick development of the c1-bishop outside the chain and accepts a slow, closed game in which Black develops comfortably.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once: it has to leave g5. Wherever it goes it leaves the queenside, so b2 is unguarded and becomes a target, and Black gains a useful tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 Qb6.strategy: Attacks the undefended b2 and the d4 pawn at once, since the bishop has left the queenside. White must spend a move on defence, and Black gets an active queen at the price of exposing it to later harassment.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 Bf5.strategy: Brings the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can lock it in. Black develops comfortably, and White's bishop on g5 has not yet found a useful job.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bh4.strategy: Keeps the bishop on the board instead of trading it, and leaves it pointing at e7 and the kingside. The price is that it is far from the queenside, where b2 has no defender at all.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bf4.strategy: Keeps the bishop outside the pawn chain and eyes the c7 and b8 squares, so its development is not wasted. Like Bh4 it leaves b2 unguarded, so Black's queen may aim at it with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bc1.strategy: Retreats to the starting square and guards b2 again, but undoes the bishop's outing: White has spent two moves to Black's one and is a tempo behind in a solid, level game.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bh4 Qb6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Levitsky Attack, Euwe Variation, Modern Line
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bh4 Qb6.strategy: Attacks b2, which the bishop on h4 no longer guards, and presses on d4 as well. White has to spend a move on defence, so Black takes the initiative on the queenside while keeping a solid pawn structure.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bh4 Bf5.strategy: Brings the bishop outside the pawn chain and develops while White's bishop is still far from the queenside. Black keeps the queen move against b2 in reserve, so White cannot rely on b2 staying unattacked.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6 3.Bg5 h6 4.Bh4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and fights for e4 and d5, but allows Bxf6, which takes a defender from d5 and leaves Black with doubled f-pawns, with the two bishops as the only compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System, with e6
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.background: The Irish-American James Mason was the first master-level player to use the London System regularly, including at Vienna 1882. The name comes from the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared seven times, and in the 21st century it has become popular among club players for its solid nature and clear plans.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Brings the dark-squared bishop out in front of the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, and eyes c7 on the way. Black's ...e6 has already hemmed in the light-squared bishop. White picks a solid development scheme and leaves the fight for the centre for later.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.c4.strategy: Brings the Queen's Gambit idea into the position: the pawn challenges d5 and White fights for queenside space, while Black holds the centre with a solid chain. The c8-bishop remains Black's problem piece, and White gets a lasting initiative on the queenside if Black cannot free it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports d4 behind a solid pawn chain, at the price of shutting in the c1-bishop for now. White keeps the choice of queenside plans open, and the game stays closed with both sides developing without contact.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4 Nf6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System, with e6
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it watches e4 and keeps White from taking space with that pawn. It commits to nothing: Black still decides how to challenge the bishop. The light-squared bishop behind its own pawns remains the piece that needs a plan.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once, the standard way to challenge this set-up. Black gains queenside space and can aim a queen at b2, which the bishop on f4 no longer guards; the c8-bishop is still shut in behind the e6 pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bf4 Bd6.strategy: Offers to trade White's bishop at once, removing the piece White's set-up is built around. After Bxd6 Qxd6 Black has a sound, compact position; the cost is that the c8-bishop is still shut in behind the e6 pawn.
